n: Who made the oldest tools is not known: Australopithecus afarensis, Kenyanthropus platyops or a species not yet identified.

Stone tools are implements shaped from stone by knapping or grinding; the oldest known, from Lomekwi near Lake Turkana in Kenya, are dated to 3.3 million years ago, about a million years before the genus Homo.
The oldest hand axe, from Konso-Gardula, could be 1.9 million years old, and early examples are dated to 1.6 million years ago in the later Oldowan.
A hand axe is a prehistoric stone tool with two faces, usually of flint or chert, shaped by knapping.
Claims reach back 1.5 to 2 million years, but traces of wood ash from about 1 million years ago are the evidence with the firmest scholarly support.

The control of fire by early humans gave warmth, light, protection from predators and a means of cooking; the earliest known controlled use of fire took place in Wonderwerk Cave, South Africa, 1.79–1.0 million years ago.
Control of fire by early humans

The earliest evidence is indirect, small stone points from Uzbekistan, Sibudu in South Africa (72,000–60,000 years ago) and elsewhere; the oldest surviving bows, from Holmegaard in Denmark, date from about 9000 BCE.
Archery is the use of bows to shoot arrows in hunting and warfare.
Bone awls from Blombos Cave in southern Africa date to 73,000–70,000 years ago, and a point from Sibudu Cave in South Africa, 61,000 years old, might be from a bone needle.
A sewing needle is a slender pointed tool with an eye at one end to carry thread through material.
Neanderthals may have burned lignite at Les Canalettes in France about 70,000 years ago.
Coal is a combustible sedimentary rock used as fuel.

A very small fragment of three-ply cord from a Neanderthal site, about 50,000 years old, is only a suspected rope, and a 35,000 to 40,000 year old ivory tool from Hohle Fels is identified as a means of making rope, not rope itself.
Rope is a group of yarns, fibres or strands twisted or braided together into a larger and stronger form, used for dragging, lifting and fastening since prehistoric times.
The earliest prehistoric tackle is the gorge, a double-pointed stick tied to a line, which anchored in the fish's gullet and worked similarly to a hook.
A fish hook is a hook used to catch fish by piercing the inside of the mouth, attached to a line and baited.
Its age, with estimates from 9000 BCE to 44,000 years ago, and whether its marks are mathematical are both debated.
The Ishango bone is an engraved bone tool found at Ishango, near the Semliki River in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and believed to be about 20,000 years old.
Fired-clay figurines are older: those of Dolní Věstonice in the Czech Republic date to 29,000–25,000 BCE.

Pottery is the craft and products of forming vessels and other objects from clay fired at high temperatures; the earliest known pottery vessels, from Xianren Cave in Jiangxi, China, date to 20,000–19,000 years ago.
When the first dome was built is not known; the mammoth-bone dwellings of Mezhirich may be the earliest. Corbelled stone domes appear in the Neolithic Near East.

A dome is an architectural element resembling the hollow upper half of a sphere; the earliest found may be four dwellings of mammoth tusks and bones at Mezhirich in Ukraine, dated between 19,280 and 11,700 BCE.

Other remains are disputed at 36,000 years ago, and the oldest known dog skeletons, from the Altai Mountains of Siberia and a cave in Belgium, are dated to about 33,000 years ago. This may indicate that domestication occurred in several places at once.
The domestication of the dog began approximately 15,000 to 30,000 years ago, when ancient wolf populations gradually adapted to human settlements.
It may be older: it is believed to have been in use from around 30,000 years ago, and the arthritic right elbow of Mungo Man, of 42,000 BP, has been read as 'atlatl elbow'.
A spear-thrower, or atlatl, is a lever, usually about as long as the user's arm or forearm, with a cup or spur that holds the butt of a dart or javelin and throws it faster than the arm alone could.
the Fertile Crescent (goats, pigs, sheep, cattle)

Domestication is a long-term relationship in which one species takes over the control and care of another to obtain resources such as meat, milk or labour; domestication by humans began with the dog at least 15,000 years ago.
Near East (sites around Israel and Wadi Ziqlab, Jordan)
The sickle is a single-handed agricultural tool with a curved blade, used for harvesting grain or cutting forage.
Starch residue on pounding rocks from 30,000 years ago in Europe and Australia suggests that a primitive flatbread was possibly made then; this is called only a possibility.
Bread is a baked food product made from water, flour, and often yeast, and is one of the oldest human-made foods.
How beer was first made is debated; the earliest chemically confirmed barley beer, from Godin Tepe in Iran, is 5,400–5,000 years old.

Beer is one of the oldest human-produced drinks, made by fermenting cereal grains; the earliest archaeological evidence of fermentation is 13,000-year-old residues of a gruel-like beer used by the Natufians for ritual feasting at Raqefet…
Ethiopia, the Sahel and West Africa
Dates for its beginning in West Asia range from about 12,000 to 8000 BCE.

The Neolithic Revolution, or First Agricultural Revolution, was the transition of many human cultures from hunting and gathering to farming and settlement, which began in the Fertile Crescent between 10,000 and 8000 BCE.
A sled, sledge or sleigh is a vehicle that slides across a surface, usually of ice or snow, built with a smooth underside or a body supported by runners that reduce friction.

Hunter-gatherers in West Asia harvested wild wheats perhaps as early as 21,000 BCE. The earliest secure evidence for domestic emmer comes from Çayönü, c. 8300 to 7600 BCE, and for domestic einkorn from after c. 8800 BCE.
Wheat is a group of wild and domesticated grasses of the genus Triticum, cultivated for their grains, which are staple foods around the world.
Mesolithic sites (stone lamps; no single place named)
Some archaeologists claim shell lamps existed more than 6,000 years ago, and the oldest stone oil lamp is said to come from Lascaux, in a cave inhabited 10,000 to 15,000 years ago.
An oil lamp is a lamp that burns an oil-based fuel, drawn up a textile wick from a container, in the same way as a candle burns solid fuel.
A mudbrick is an air-dried, unfired brick of mud mixed with a binder such as straw or rice husks, first known from the dwellings of Jericho, dated to 9000 BCE.

Grinding stones for vegetal food, and possibly flour, were widespread across Europe from at least 30,000 years ago, and a prehistoric quern from Longwangchan in Shaanxi, China, is dated to 23,000 BCE, earlier than the Abu Hureyra find.
A quern-stone is a stone tool for hand-grinding grain and other materials, used in pairs: a lower stationary stone and an upper stone moved across it.
Net sinkers from 27,000 BCE found in Korea are the oldest fishing implements known, but they are weights, not a net.
A fishing net is a net used to catch fish, usually a mesh of knotted thread that serves as an improvised trap.
Techniques indistinguishable from rope making are evidenced since the earliest hominin presence in South Africa, but no specimens survive.
Basket weaving is the process of weaving or sewing pliable materials such as willow, grasses, vines and splints into baskets, mats and similar objects.

Clay tokens are small shaped pieces of clay that stood for animals and goods, first used to keep records in the ancient Near East around 8000–7500 BCE; the earliest known come from the Zagros region of Iran.
Dugouts may be the oldest boats found only because their massive wood survives better than lighter craft such as bark canoes.
A dugout canoe, or logboat, is a boat made from a hollowed-out tree, and the oldest boat type archaeologists have found.
Kuk Swamp is an archaeological site in the Wahgi Valley of the Papua New Guinea highlands, at about 1,550 metres, some 12–13 kilometres northeast of Mount Hagen.

The Kakinoshima pieces are also dated to the 9th millennium BCE, and a lacquer tree of the Jōmon period is 12,600 years old. Experts are divided on whether Jōmon lacquer was invented independently or derived from Chinese techniques.
Lacquerware consists of objects coated with lacquer, in East Asia an urushiol-based lacquer from the dried sap of the lacquer tree, Toxicodendron vernicifluum.
Maize is a cereal crop domesticated in Mesoamerica, the staple of the Aztec and other American civilisations.
Estimates for its domestication in China range from 13,500 to 8,200 years ago.
Rice is a cereal grain cultivated in flooded paddies or dry fields and is a staple food across much of Asia and parts of West Africa.
North-central China (between the Yellow and Huai rivers)

The origin is debated: some evidence points to low-intensity cultivation across several places in East Asia before the Chinese lineage dominated. The first unambiguously domesticated, large-seeded soybeans come from Daundong in Korea, and the oldest preserved modern-looking ones from about 1000 BCE.
The soybean is a species of legume native to East Asia, widely grown for its edible bean.
Lake Titicaca region, Peru and Bolivia
The potato is a starchy tuber native to the Andes of South America, spread worldwide after the Spanish conquest.
Estimates of the earliest trepanation vary from 10,000 to 7,000 years ago.

Trepanning, or trepanation, is a surgical intervention in which a hole is drilled or scraped into the human skull, perhaps the oldest surgical procedure with archaeological evidence; at a burial site in France dated to 6500 BCE, 40 of 120…
Skis are runners designed to glide over snow, used in pairs and fastened to the boots by bindings.
Solnitsata in Bulgaria is also said to have supplied salt from 5400 BCE; that is later than the Romanian evidence.
Salt is a mineral composed mainly of sodium chloride, used as a seasoning and as a preservative for meat and fish.
Cotton is a plant fibre spun and woven into textiles, one of the most important traded commodities in history.
Irrigation is the practice of applying controlled amounts of water to land to help grow crops, with some of the earliest known use dating to the 6th millennium BCE in Khuzistan, south-west Iran.
A mirror is an object that reflects an image.

The exact date and location of olive tree domestication are unclear; wild olives are reported to have been collected by Neolithic people as early as the 8th millennium BCE, and that the earliest surviving olive oil amphorae date to 3500 BCE in Early Minoan times.
Olive oil is the oil pressed from olives, a staple of Mediterranean diet, lighting and trade since antiquity.

Pottery jars from Jiahu in China, of the early seventh millennium BCE, may have held a fermented drink of rice and grapes, but other fruits cannot be ruled out. The Hajj Firuz jars from Iran, of about 5000 BCE, are also called the earliest firm evidence of wine production.
Wine is an alcoholic drink made by fermenting grapes.
Taiwan and Island Southeast Asia (Austronesian sails)
When and where the sail was invented is not known; many date it no earlier than the 5th millennium BCE.

A sail is a tensile structure of fabric or another membrane that uses the wind to propel a craft; sailing boats appear on Cucuteni–Trypillian ceramics from the 6th millennium BCE, and excavations of the Ubaid period in Mesopotamia give…
Holed pottery from pile-dwellings on Lake Neuchatel in Switzerland, roughly eight thousand years old, is thought to come from cheese strainers; where cheese-making began is not known.
Cheese is a food made by curdling milk.
A copper axe from Prokuplje in Serbia may be older, c. 5500 BCE, and smelting may have begun separately in Asia and in Europe.
Copper smelting is the production of copper from its ores at high temperature; the world's oldest securely dated evidence for it, from c. 5000 BCE, was found at Belovode on Rudnik mountain in Serbia.

Evidence at Neolithic sites in the Fertile Crescent dates to the 9th to 7th millennium BCE, which would be earlier than the Chinese sites, but no dated site is given, so the card uses the explicit date of 5000 BCE.
Rammed earth, also called pisé, is a technique for building foundations, floors and walls by compacting a damp mixture of natural raw materials such as earth, chalk, lime or gravel into a formwork.
Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin, and the term is also used loosely for related copper alloys such as brass.
San Andrés, Gulf of Mexico lowlands

Wild progenitor populations are centred in west-central Brazil, where cassava was likely first domesticated no more than 10,000 years ago. The oldest direct evidence of cultivation comes from the Maya site of Joya de Cerén in El Salvador, 1,400 years old.
Cassava, also called manioc, is a starchy root crop native to South America.
Fired bricks are also said to have been used only since c. 4000 BCE. In China proper brick construction of walls and vaults emerged only in the third century BCE.
Fired brick is brick of clay and shale baked in a kiln, harder and longer-lasting than the older sun-dried mudbrick.
Many scholars credit the Sumerians of Mesopotamia; south-eastern Europe, China and Egypt have also been proposed.

The potter's wheel is a machine for shaping, or throwing, clay into round ceramic ware; the oldest found, from the Cucuteni–Trypillia culture in western Ukraine, dates to the middle of the 5th millennium BCE.
The warp-weighted loom may have originated earlier, in the Neolithic period.
A loom is a device for weaving cloth and tapestry that holds the warp threads under tension while the weft threads are passed over and under them.
Indigo is a blue dye obtained from plants, widely used to colour textiles.
Lime mortar is a masonry mortar made of lime and an aggregate such as sand, mixed with water.
Wheeled vehicles appear almost together in Mesopotamia, the Caucasus and Europe in the 4th millennium BCE; whether they spread from the Near East is debated.

A wheel is a rotating component, usually circular, that turns on an axle; the oldest indirect evidence of wheeled movement, miniature clay wheels found north of the Black Sea, dates from before 4000 BCE.
H. V. Hilprecht dated the Nippur arch to before 4000 BCE.
An arch is a curved structure spanning an opening, bearing the load above it or serving as decoration, first known in the ancient Near East, where the Nippur arch was built before 3800 BCE.

Historians believe snowshoes were invented 4,000 to 6,000 years ago, probably in Central Asia. Jacqui Wood has suggested that the Chalcolithic mummy Ötzi's equipment, read as a backpack frame, was part of a snowshoe.
Snowshoes are footwear with a large footprint that spreads the wearer's weight so that the wearer travels largely on top of snow.
A Confucian text dates silk to about 2700 BCE; archaeology points to the Yangshao period, 5000–3000 BCE.
Sericulture is the raising of silkworms for the production of raw silk, typically by feeding them on mulberry leaves.
Mehrgarh is said to have tanned between 7000 and 3300 BCE, a range too wide to date the start. Leather working tools about 400,000 years old at Hoxne, England, show leather working, not tanning.

Tanning is the process of treating the skins and hides of animals to produce leather, permanently altering the protein structure of the skin so that it is more durable and less liable to decomposition.
Cacao is the tree native to tropical Mesoamerica whose beans are used to make chocolate.
The article notes a contrarian view that the clay tokens were not the precursor of writing, and says the meaning and usage of the tokens are still a matter of debate.
Cuneiform is a writing system of wedge-shaped signs pressed into clay tablets, invented in Mesopotamia in the late fourth millennium BCE.
A slightly shorter yew bow from Rotten Bottom, Tweedsmuir, Scotland, has a calibrated radiocarbon date of 4040 to 3640 BCE; European longbows are also said to date from the Paleolithic.
A longbow is a tall bow that makes a long draw possible, usually a self bow cut from a single piece of wood.

One dating gives about 1600 BCE for the earliest specimens, while another dates the first weapons that can be called swords to about 3300 BCE at Arslantepe; the first swords beyond ambiguity are Minoan, from about 1700 BCE.
A sword is an edged weapon intended for manual cutting or thrusting, with a blade longer than that of a knife or dagger.
The pigment is also said to have been first synthesised in the Fourth Dynasty. Whether its presence beyond Egypt reflects its spread or parallel invention is unclear.
Egyptian blue, a calcium copper silicate, is a pigment made by heating silica, lime, a copper compound and an alkali, and is considered the first synthetic pigment.
Whether hieroglyphs arose independently or from Mesopotamian writing is debated; signs from Abydos as early as 3400 BCE question Mesopotamian priority.
Egyptian hieroglyphs were the formal writing system of ancient Egypt, using pictorial signs for sounds and words.
Corbelling was first applied by the ancient Egyptians and Chaldeans, but no date is given for that; the earliest dated example is Newgrange, built between 3200 and 2500 BCE.

A corbel arch is an arch-like construction in which successive horizontal courses of stone or brick are offset from the springline of the walls, each projecting towards the centre until the courses meet at the apex.

Beekeeping in pottery vessels is also reported beginning about 9,000 years ago in Anatolia, beeswax traces in Middle East potsherds from about 7,000 BCE, and depictions of honey collecting about 10,000 years ago; 3,100 BCE is given as the first evidence from Egypt of beekeeping being practised.
Beekeeping, or apiculture, is the maintenance of bee colonies, commonly in artificial beehives, to collect honey and other products such as beeswax and propolis.
Serrated tools showing signs of cutting wood from Pech-de-l'Azé cave IV in France are dated 90,000 to 30,000 years BCE; Chinese legend credits Lu Ban and Greek myth credits Talos.
A saw is a tool with a tough blade, wire or chain bearing a hard toothed edge, used to cut wood, metal or stone.
A dam is a structure that impounds water or restricts its flow.
Outriggers may first have been needed after the crab claw sail appeared, around 1500 BCE.

An outrigger canoe is a boat steadied by one or more side floats, or outriggers, fastened to its hull; such boats were developed by the Austronesian-speaking peoples of the islands of Southeast Asia, and they enabled the Austronesian…
It was used at least as far back as the First Dynasty; the oldest written papyri yet found, the Diary of Merer, date from about 2560 BCE.
Papyrus is a writing material made from the pith of the papyrus plant, which grew abundantly in the Nile valley and delta.

The wood and leather toe from a burial near Thebes, dated 950 to 710 BCE, is described as the first confirmed use of a prosthetic device, as it shows wear; before its discovery in 2000 the oldest known was an artificial leg from Capua.
A prosthesis is an artificial device that replaces a missing body part lost through injury, disease or a condition present at birth.

The oldest radiocarbon-dated remains, 8080 BCE, come from caves in the Chilca Canyon in Peru, but they are given as remains, not as domesticated plants. Sweet potato in Polynesia, radiocarbon-dated to 1210 to 1400 CE in the Cook Islands, is explained by pre-Columbian contact, a model the present scholarly consensus favours.
The sweet potato is a starchy root crop native to the Americas that spread across the world after the sixteenth century through Spanish and Portuguese trade networks.
Ox-drawn ards may go back to the 6th millennium BCE in Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley.

A plough is a farm tool for loosening or turning soil before sowing; ploughs were at first powered by people, and the larger ox-drawn ard, or scratch plough, followed the domestication of oxen in Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley, perhaps…
Who first made true soap, as distinct from earlier soap-like mixtures, is uncertain; Pliny the Elder called it an invention of the Gauls.

Soap is a salt of a fatty acid, often made by mixing fats or oils with an alkali, used for washing and cleaning; the earliest recorded evidence of soap-like materials comes from Mesopotamia, c. 2800 BCE.
Some Egyptologists think the nearby enclosure wall Gisr el-Mudir is older; the credit to Imhotep is that of modern Egyptologists.
The Pyramid of Djoser, or Step Pyramid, is a six-stepped stone pyramid at Saqqara in Egypt, built for the Third Dynasty king Djoser in the 27th century BCE.

Water-flushed latrines are said to exist since the Neolithic: Skara Brae in Orkney (c. 31st century BCE) had drains that washed waste away, and in 2023 a flush toilet about 2,400 years old was reported from Xi'an, China. Harington's 1596 design and Cumming's 1775 S-trap are the forerunners of the modern form.
A flush toilet disposes of human waste by collecting it in a bowl and using the force of water to channel it through a drainpipe.
The earliest Chinese inks may date to four millennia ago, in the Neolithic, but direct evidence for inksticks is from around 256 BCE.
Ink is a gel, sol or solution containing a colourant, used to colour a surface to produce an image, text or design.
The form of the Sumerian device is unknown; the oldest surviving counting board, the Salamis Tablet, dates from about 300 BCE.

An abacus, or counting frame, is a hand-operated calculating tool of beads or counters moved on a board or rods, first known in Sumer, where it appeared between 2700 and 2300 BCE with columns for the orders of magnitude of the base-60…

Otto Neugebauer held that the origins of sexagesimal are not as simple, consistent, or singular in time as they are often portrayed, its use always mixing in a strong undercurrent of decimal notation.
Sexagesimal, or base 60, is a numeral system with sixty as its base, which originated with the Sumerians in the 3rd millennium BCE and passed to the Babylonians.
The earliest glass objects are often counted as faience; true glass appears in the 15th century BCE.
Glassmaking is the craft of producing glass objects.
Other early claims are tentative or disputed, at Kaman-Kalehöyük in Turkey (2200–2000 BCE) and Lejja in Nigeria; the old idea of a Hittite monopoly on iron-working is no longer accepted.
Iron smelting is the extraction of iron from ore by heating it in a furnace.

Modified stones thought to be sling ammunition are reported from the Near East as early as the 6th millennium BCE, and a possible slinger appears at Catalhoyuk, c. 7000 BCE, but the slings themselves rarely survive.
The sling is a simple projectile weapon consisting of a cord and pouch used to hurl stones or lead shot.
Chinese tradition credits the wife of Lu Ban in the Warring States Period.
An umbrella is a folding canopy supported by ribs on a pole, used against sun or rain.

Pliny the Elder's account that parchment was invented at Pergamon to replace papyrus is almost assuredly false, since parchment was in use in Anatolia and elsewhere long before Pergamon. A first mention of Egyptian leather documents goes back to the Fourth Dynasty (c. 2550–2450 BCE).
Parchment is a writing material made from specially prepared untanned skins of animals, primarily sheep, calves and goats; the finer form made from calfskin is called vellum.
Earlier claims, at Botai in Kazakhstan (3700–3500 BCE) and on the steppe in the 5th millennium BCE, are debated.

The domestication of the horse turned wild horses into domestic animals; genomic evidence places the source of all modern domestic horses in the Volga–Don region of the Pontic–Caspian steppe, in present-day southwestern Russia, around…
Some historians hold that it began on the Nile, citing tomb drawings at Thebes from 1250 BCE; another theory, with little evidence, places its origin in India.

The shadoof is a tool for lifting water from a well, river or pond onto land or into a channel: a long pole pivoted on an upright frame, with a bucket at one end and a counterweight of clay or stone at the other.
The origin of terracing in the Andes is poorly understood.
An andén (plural andenes) is a stair-step terrace dug into a hillside for farming, built by pre-Columbian cultures in the Andes by 2000 BCE.
Early aqueducts were also built in the Indian subcontinent, Greece, the Near East and the Nile valley.
An aqueduct is a channel or structure built to carry water from a source to a city, often across valleys on arches.
When and where it began is not known; the bows in the tomb of Tutankhamun, who died in 1324 BCE, are among the earliest dated.
A composite bow is a bow made from layers of wood, horn and sinew glued together, giving great power in a short length suitable for use on horseback.

Perfumery began in Mesopotamia, Egypt, the Indus Valley and possibly ancient China, with no date given for the start. The Indus civilisation is given as 3300 BCE to 1300 BCE, which is not a date for perfume itself.
Perfume is a mixture of fragrant essential oils or aroma compounds, fixatives and solvents, used to give an agreeable scent to the body, objects and living spaces.
A mobile siege tower is shown in the First Intermediate Period tomb of General Intef at Thebes, Egypt, which is not dated more closely.
A siege tower is a mobile wooden tower used to bring attackers to the top of fortification walls.
The earliest traces are at Dholavira, a city of the Indus Valley Civilisation; Ashoka’s inscriptions describe stepwells along the roads, and the first rock-cut ones date from 200–400 CE.
A stepwell, or vav, is a well, cistern or pond reached by a long corridor of steps down to the water, developed in India, where the earliest archaeological evidence is at Dholavira.
Some scholars class the Sintashta vehicles as carts and see the chariot as a Near Eastern invention of the early 2nd millennium BCE.
A chariot is a light, two-wheeled, horse-drawn vehicle used in warfare, carrying a driver and an archer or spearman.
A pulley is a wheel on an axle or shaft that lets a taut cable or belt passing over it move and change direction, or transfer power between itself and a shaft.
An early date of about 1850 BCE and a late one of about 1550 BCE are debated, which decides whether the alphabet arose in Egypt or in Canaan.

The Proto-Sinaitic script is the earliest known trace of alphabetic writing, found in about 30–40 inscriptions at Serabit el-Khadim in Sinai and in two at Wadi el-Hol in Middle Egypt dated to between 1900 and 1800 BCE.
The Minoans may have pioneered the dye; the Phoenicians of Tyre, after whom it is named, may have used it from about 1570 BCE.
Tyrian purple is a deep purple dye produced from murex sea snails, named after the Phoenician city of Tyre.

The article also gives earlier or vaguer dates, none presented as secure: lunar omens in 'reports from Nineveh and Babylon, circa 2500-670 B.C.', Venus observations that 'probably' go back to the second millennium BC but survive in a 7th-century BC copy (the Venus tablet of Ammisaduqa), and the Omen Compendia, composed from the beginning of the second millennium onwards.
Babylonian astronomy refers to the systematic observation and mathematical prediction of celestial phenomena developed in ancient Mesopotamia, flourishing under Chaldean patronage.
Possible evidence of felting at Çatal Hüyük in Anatolia about 6000 BCE is not firm; the origin is said to have been most likely in east Asia.
Felt is a textile made by matting, condensing and pressing fibres, such as wool or animal fur, together.

The Egyptian Berlin Papyrus 6619, also written c. 1800 BCE, solves a problem with the triple 6:8:10 but does not mention a triangle. The theorem is named for Pythagoras (c. 570 to c. 495 BCE), yet no specific attribution to him exists in surviving Greek literature from the five centuries after his life.

The Pythagorean theorem is a relation in Euclidean geometry between the three sides of a right triangle: the area of the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the areas of the squares on the other two sides.
The surviving copy may reproduce an older original of the Old Kingdom; the suggestion that Imhotep wrote it is conjecture.

The Edwin Smith Papyrus is an ancient Egyptian medical text and the oldest known surgical treatise on trauma, copied c. 1600 BCE, probably at Thebes, from an original that may date from the Old Kingdom.

Rubber is an elastic material produced from the latex of certain tropical trees, which became an important industrial commodity in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries with the growth of bicycles, automobiles and electrical…

The use of water clocks in Babylonian astronomy is traced back to the Old Babylonian Empire (c. 2000–1600 BCE), and N. Narahari Achar and Subhash Kak suggest their use in India as early as the 2nd millennium BCE from the Atharvaveda.
A water clock, or clepsydra, measures time by the regulated flow of water into or out of a vessel.
A sundial tells the time of day from the apparent position of the Sun, usually by the shadow that a gnomon casts on a dial marked with hour-lines.

Arthur Evans dated the Knossos archive to a fire of about 1400 BCE; after Carl Blegen's excavation at Pylos in 1939 the date was questioned, and there has been no generally accepted resolution. The Kafkania pebble, from an earlier context, is not genuine.
Linear B is the syllabic script used by the Mycenaean palaces of Greece and Crete from about 1450 to 1200 BCE to record an early form of Greek.
The first single-tube seed drills may go back to Sumer.
A seed drill is a device that sows seeds by placing them in the soil at a set depth; the Babylonians used primitive seed drills around 1400 BCE.
Its mature form implies earlier development, but no older writing has been found.

The oracle bone script is the oldest attested form of written Chinese, carved mostly on ox shoulder bones and turtle plastrons for the Late Shang royal family from the 13th century BCE; inscriptions of King Wu Ding's reign are radiocarbon…

Distillation is the separation of the substances in a liquid mixture by selective boiling and the condensation of the vapours in a still; Akkadian tablets of c. 1200 BCE describing perfumery show that a primitive form was known to the…
Tobacco is the common name of plants of the genus Nicotiana and of any product prepared from their cured leaves.
No Phoenician inscription is securely dated before the 10th century BCE.
The Phoenician alphabet is a script of 22 consonant letters, written from right to left, used in Phoenicia and across the Mediterranean for most of the 1st millennium BCE.
Some sources propose an origin in south-east Arabia, and the dating of the Peruvian puquios is disputed.
A qanat is an underground channel that carries water by gravity from mountain aquifers to lowland fields and settlements.
Scissors are hand-operated cutting tools made of a pair of pivoting blades whose sharpened edges slide past each other.
A screw is a helically threaded fastener tightened or released by twisting its head, and one of the six classical simple machines.
A possible battering ram, carried by soldiers under a mobile roofed structure, is shown in the tomb of the 11th Dynasty Egyptian noble Khety; it is said only that the pole may represent a simple ram.
A battering ram is a siege weapon consisting of a heavy beam used to break down gates and walls.
The oldest substantial inscriptions date from about 740 BCE.
The Greek alphabet is the script of the Greek language, in use since the late 9th or early 8th century BCE (conventionally about 800 BCE), with early samples from at least 775 BCE.
Whether Europe's blast furnaces of the 12th and 13th centuries arose independently or from Chinese knowledge is uncertain.

Cast iron is an iron–carbon alloy with more than 2% carbon, valued for its relatively low melting temperature; the earliest known cast-iron artefacts, from what is now Jiangsu in China, date to the 8th century BCE.
There is disputed evidence that humans began riding the horse not long after domestication, possibly as early as 4000 BCE, and that a saddle-like blanket probably came first.
A saddle is a supportive structure for a rider, fastened to an animal's back by a girth.
A chain pump is a water pump in which circular discs or square pallets are fixed to an endless chain.
Whether it came from Greece (Corinth, by Thucydides) or Phoenicia (Sidon) is disputed; triremes are first definitely recorded in battle about 525 BCE.

The trireme was an ancient Mediterranean galley driven by three banks of oars with one man to each oar, first referred to at the end of the 8th century BCE; scholars are divided on whether it came from Greece or Phoenicia.
A similar library was found in 1849 in the palace of Sennacherib (705–681 BCE), and because the tablets of the two were mixed after reaching Europe, the contents of each can hardly be reconstructed.

The Library of Ashurbanipal is a collection of more than 30,000 clay tablets and fragments of the 7th century BCE, gathered at Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, by Ashurbanipal, king of the Neo-Assyrian Empire from 668 to 627 BCE.

It is unclear when and where candles were first used; objects that could be candlesticks were found in Babylonian and Minoan contexts and in the tomb of Tutankhamun, but the early 'candles' may have been plant material dipped in fat.
A candle is an ignitable wick embedded in wax or another flammable solid such as tallow, which gives light.
Some trace the crossbow and its name into China from Austroasiatic peoples in the 4th century BCE, but older locks from Zhou tombs contradict this.
A crossbow is a bow mounted horizontally on a stock, shot by a trigger mechanism, allowing troops with limited training to shoot powerful bolts.
Guanzhuang in China is the oldest securely dated minting site, and Aegina has also been proposed for the first coins.

Coinage is the minting of small metal pieces for use as money, first known in the 7th century BCE in China, where a factory at Guanzhuang in Henan made shovel-shaped bronze coins between 640 and 550 BCE, and in Anatolia, where the…

According to tradition it was first built around 600 BCE on the orders of the king Tarquinius Priscus; otherwise it is said only to have been built during either the Roman Kingdom or the early Roman Republic.
The Cloaca Maxima ('Greatest Sewer') is one of the oldest sewer systems in the world, built in ancient Rome to drain the marshy valley of the Forum into the Tiber.
Tenuous evidence of a turned artifact at a Mycenaean Greek site may go back to the 13th or 14th century BCE.
A lathe is a machine tool that turns a workpiece about an axis while tools cut, sand, drill or shape it into a form symmetrical about that axis.

The date is not entirely clear: Herodotus mentions the tunnel in his account of the tyrant Polycrates, who ruled c. 540 to 522 BCE, but does not say he built it. It is called the second known tunnel excavated from both ends.
The Tunnel of Eupalinos is an aqueduct tunnel 1,036 metres long cut through Mount Kastro on Samos in the sixth century BCE, under the tyrant Polycrates.

It is uncertain when elephant warfare started, and riding elephants in peace and war is believed to be much older than recorded history; the Vedic epics depict it but are dated only to the 5th-4th century BCE.
A war elephant is an elephant trained for combat, used to charge enemy formations, carry archers and intimidate opponents.
The shaduf of ancient Mesopotamia is sometimes counted as the first crane, but it was a lever for lifting irrigation water.
A crane is a machine that lifts and moves loads with a boom, hoist, ropes or chains and sheaves, using levers and pulleys for mechanical advantage.
The iron plough, or iron-tipped plough, is a plough whose cutting edge is made of iron, allowing deeper and more efficient tillage.

The Shi Jing records King Wen of Zhou building the first pontoon bridge in the 11th century BCE, but Joseph Needham holds that the temporary pontoon bridge was invented in China in the 9th or 8th century BCE, since that part of the text was probably added later. The Chhun Chhiu Hou Chuan places its invention in the Qin state in 257 BCE.
A pontoon bridge, also called a floating bridge, uses floats or shallow-draft boats to support a continuous deck for pedestrians and vehicles.
Its western sections may first have been built by the Assyrian kings.
The Royal Road was an ancient highway of the Achaemenid Empire running about 2,700 kilometres from Susa to Sardis, with relay stations along its length.

The three-field system is a crop rotation in which a field bears one set of crops in the first year, another in the second, and lies fallow in the third; it was first used in China in the Eastern Zhou period.
A yurt, or ger, is a portable round tent covered and insulated with skins or felt, traditionally used as a dwelling by nomadic groups in the steppes and mountains of Inner Asia.
Its oldest sections were dug by the states of Wu and Yue from 486 BCE; Emperor Yang of Sui joined them into one network in 604–609.
The Grand Canal is a vast system of waterways in China linking the Yangtze region with the north.

The Gunditjmara of south-western Victoria, Australia, may have raised eels at Budj Bim as early as about 4,580 BCE, though Peter Sutton disputes that their eel traps were aquaculture. Evidence from Jiahu in China, from 6200 BCE, is speculative.
Aquaculture is the farming of fish, crustaceans, molluscs, algae and other aquatic organisms under controlled or semi-natural conditions.
The Bible credits King Uzziah of Judah with stone-throwing machines about 750 BCE, but in a much later text.
A catapult is a siege engine that hurls projectiles using tension, torsion or human traction, used before gunpowder artillery.
None of its some 60 texts is proven to be by Hippocrates himself.

The Hippocratic Corpus is a collection of around 60 early Greek medical works associated with the physician Hippocrates, most written in the last decades of the 5th century BCE and the first half of the 4th; none is proven to be his own.
Its origins may lie in Carthaginian Sardinia, and the hand-powered rotary mill, used by the Carthaginians as early as the 6th century BCE, may have led to it.
A horse mill is a mill that uses a horse engine as its power source, most often to grind grain or pump water; donkeys, oxen and camels can drive such mills too.

The article mentions possible earlier traces: perforated gnomons projecting a pinhole image of the sun in the Chinese Zhoubi Suanjing (1046 BC–256 BC, with material added until c. 220 AD), and theories that camera obscura effects inspired Paleolithic cave paintings or played a role in Neolithic structures.

A camera obscura is a dark chamber or box in which light passing through a small hole projects an inverted image of the scene outside onto the opposite surface; one of the earliest known written records of the effect is the Chinese text…

Gears appear in works connected to Hero of Alexandria, but are traced back to the mechanics of the Library of Alexandria in the 3rd century BCE and to Archimedes (287 to 212 BCE); these are accounts of use, and the earliest surviving gears are the Chinese ones.
A gear is a rotating machine part with teeth that engage the teeth of another part to transmit rotational motion or torque.
Some accounts date the noria proper from around 300 CE, when the Romans replaced its wooden compartments with ceramic pots tied to the outside of an open-framed wheel.
A noria is a water wheel turned by a river's current whose rim carries pots, buckets or compartments that lift water into a small aqueduct, for irrigation or to supply towns.
The trebuchet is a siege engine that uses a pivoting arm to hurl heavy projectiles, either by human traction or by a heavy counterweight.
The first watermills have been placed in Persia before 350 BCE and in Byzantium and Alexandria in the 3rd century BCE.

A water wheel is a machine that turns the energy of flowing or falling water into power through a large wheel with blades or buckets on its rim; it first appeared in ancient Egypt in the 4th century BCE, where wheels lifted water for…
Securely proven production sites are later: Sri Lanka in the 6th to 10th centuries CE and southern India from the 16th; the early evidence from Kodumanal is preliminary.

Crucible steel is steel made by melting iron, often with fluxes, in a crucible, which allows precise control of its carbon content; it was first developed in southern India and Sri Lanka by the wootz process, with material as early as 300…
It is largely a compilation of earlier Greek mathematics, and how much of it Euclid wrote himself is debated.
Euclid's Elements is a mathematical treatise in 13 books written about 300 BCE by the Greek mathematician Euclid, the oldest surviving large-scale deductive treatment of mathematics.
Livy mentions roads near Rome as early as about 500 BCE, but they are taken to have been little more than levelled earthen tracks.
Roman roads were the network of routes built from about 300 BCE through the expansion of the Roman Republic and later the Roman Empire, carrying armies, officials, messages and trade overland.
Pliny the Elder named Sostratus of Cnidus as its architect, but that is disputed.
The Lighthouse of Alexandria, or Pharos, was a tower built on the island of Pharos at Alexandria in Egypt under the first Ptolemaic kings and completed around 280 BCE.
Copernicus revived it as predictive astronomy in 1543; whether Aryabhata’s system of 499 was heliocentric is debated.

Heliocentrism is a superseded astronomical model that placed the Sun at the centre of the universe, with the Earth and the planets orbiting it; the first person known to have proposed it was Aristarchus of Samos, c. 270 BCE.

The Assyriologist Stephanie Dalley argued from an inscription of Sennacherib that bronze water screws irrigated the Hanging Gardens of Babylon; John Peter Oleson notes there is no literary or archaeological evidence for the screw before about 250 BCE. Some scholars think Archimedes found Egyptians already using it.
An Archimedes' screw is a hydraulic machine of an outer cylinder and an inner cylinder with helical blades, used to lift water from low-lying water into irrigation ditches and for drainage.
Joseph Needham traced the Chinese armillary sphere to the single-ring instrument of Shi Shen and Gan De in the 4th century BCE, a dating that Christopher Cullen rejects.
An armillary sphere is a model of the sky made of rings that stand for the celestial equator, the ecliptic and other circles, centred on the Earth or the Sun.
Most scholars derive it from a Semitic script, usually Aramaic; earlier inscribed potsherds from Sri Lanka and Tamil Nadu are disputed.

Brahmi is a writing system of ancient India that appeared as a fully developed script in the 3rd century BCE; its earliest securely dated inscriptions are the rock-cut edicts of Ashoka, from 250–232 BCE.
The modern concept is attributed to Honoré Blanc (c. 1778) and the Gribeauval system (1765); Eli Whitney's demonstration of 1801 is an early attempt rather than the first.
Interchangeable parts are components made to specifications so nearly identical that any one fits an assembly of the same type without custom fitting.
Etruscan mail of the 4th century BCE is older, and the Avesta already mentions mail.
Chain mail is armour made of small interlocking metal rings.
It was long thought that the Maya took writing from the Olmec or Epi-Olmec; murals found in 2005 make an independent invention possible.

Maya script, or Maya glyphs, is the writing system of the Maya civilisation of Mesoamerica, known from inscriptions of the 3rd century BCE at late Preclassic sites such as San Bartolo in Guatemala and Chakjobon in Mexico.

The accuracy depends on the length of the stadion, which remains debated; with a stadion of 155 to 160 metres his value for the meridian of 252,000 stadia has an error between -2.4% and +0.8%. Cleomedes's simplified account gives 250,000 stadia, and his assumptions that Syene lies on the Tropic of Cancer and on the same meridian as Alexandria are inaccurate.
Eratosthenes made the first known scientific measurement of Earth's circumference around 240 BCE in Ptolemaic Egypt.
Paper is traditionally credited to the court official Cai Lun in 105 CE, but older paper has been found, so its first date and inventor are unknown.
Papermaking is the craft of producing paper from plant fibres, invented in China.
Its date and place of making are disputed: estimates run from 205 to 87 BCE, and Corinth’s colonies, Pergamon and Rhodes have been proposed.

The Antikythera mechanism is an ancient Greek hand-powered orrery, a geared model of the Solar System, built in the 2nd century BCE and recovered in 1901 from a shipwreck off the Greek island of Antikythera.
Rome (first in the harbours near Baiae)
Some scholars think it was developed a century earlier.
Roman concrete, or opus caementicium, is a building material used in ancient Rome: a hydraulic-setting cement mixed with an aggregate, in widespread use from about 150 BCE.
Tea drinking may be far older, under the Shang and in Yunnan, but early words for it are uncertain, and its discovery by Shennong is legend.
Tea is a beverage made from the leaves of the tea plant, native to southern China.
Trigonometry is the branch of mathematics that relates the angles of triangles to the lengths of their sides.
Its origin is disputed: some date it to about 600 BCE, and its absence from the Mawangdui texts of 198 BCE suggests a later start.

Acupuncture is a practice of traditional Chinese medicine in which thin needles are inserted into the body, believed to have originated in China around 100 BCE, when the Huangdi Neijing first documented a system of diagnosis and treatment…
The earliest reference suggests that the Temple of Ephesus was heated in this way in 350 BCE, and Garrett G. Fagan has disputed Orata’s priority.
A hypocaust is a system of central heating in which hot air and smoke from a furnace circulate beneath a floor raised on stacks of tiles, the pilae, and rise through clay or tile flues in the walls.

Glassblowing is the technique of inflating molten glass into a bubble with a blowpipe and shaping it, developed by Phoenician and Syrian craftsmen in the 1st century BCE, in what are now Lebanon and Israel.
Partial bronze plate was used by the ancient Greeks as early as the late Bronze Age (the Dendra panoply) but no date is given; full steel plate suits are a European development of about 1420.
Plate armour is body armour made from bronze, iron or steel plates, which at its fullest enclosed all or most of the wearer.
The Julian calendar is a solar calendar introduced by Julius Caesar in 46 BCE, with a leap year every four years.
The earliest date is uncertain: Takalik Abaj Stela 2 may be older, and the San Bartolo text of about 300 BCE may be the earliest Long Count notation.
The Mesoamerican Long Count calendar counts the days elapsed since a fixed starting date in 3114 BCE, using units based on twenty.
The article allows that a courier service may have existed for a time under the Roman Republic, but says the clearest reference, by Suetonius, states that Augustus created the system.
The cursus publicus was the state courier and transport service of the Roman Empire, established by Augustus, with relay stations along the main roads.
The process has its origin as early as the 5th century BCE in China, where cast iron was already in use, but the earliest extant blast furnaces are of the 1st century CE.
A blast furnace is a metallurgical furnace in which air is supplied above atmospheric pressure to smelt ore, generally iron ore into pig iron.
Vitruvius described aeolipiles earlier, about 30–20 BCE; both drew on the work of Ctesibius.

An aeolipile, or Hero's engine, is a simple bladeless steam turbine, a vessel that spins as steam escapes through bent nozzles, described by Hero of Alexandria in the 1st century CE and usually credited to him.
Whether the Western, Chinese and Indian traditions share an origin is an open question.

Alchemy is a philosophical and protoscientific tradition whose common aims were turning base metals into gold and making an elixir of immortality; in its Western form it is first attested in texts written in Greco-Roman Egypt in the first…
A papyrus codex from Ptolemaic Egypt may be older.
A codex is a book of pages stacked and bound at one edge, the ancestor of the modern book, first described in the 1st century CE, when the Roman poet Martial praised its convenience.
Some count the steering oars of Egypt and Rome as rudders; Joseph Needham held that the sternpost rudder reached Europe from China.
A sternpost rudder is a steering blade hung at the centre of a ship's stern, first known from pottery models of Chinese junks of the 1st century CE, under the Han dynasty.

Pre-Columbian Native Americans are said to have made early hypodermic needles and syringes from hollow bird bones and small animal bladders, but no date is given. Blaise Pascal invented a syringe in 1650 (not necessarily hypodermic).
A syringe is a simple reciprocating pump with a plunger fitting tightly in a cylindrical barrel, used to take in and expel liquid or gas and, in medicine, to give injections.

Chinese legend ascribes tofu to Prince Liu An (179 to 122 BCE) of Anhui province, though reliable sources for the period are few. Some scholars hold that tofu under the Han was rudimentary and lacked the firmness to count as tofu.
Tofu, or bean curd, is a food made by pressing the curds of coagulated soy milk into solid blocks.

The Records of the Three Kingdoms credit Zhuge Liang with its invention in 231 CE; M. J. T. Lewis read a 'one-wheeler' in temple inventories at Eleusis of 408–406 BCE as a Greek wheelbarrow, but there is no evidence for it in Greece or Rome.
A wheelbarrow is a small hand-propelled vehicle, usually with one wheel, pushed and guided by a single person using two handles at the rear.
By stricter definitions, whiteness and translucency, porcelain begins in the late Sui and early Tang; Shang dynasty wares are called proto-porcelain.
Porcelain is a fine, hard, translucent ceramic first developed in China.

Unverified claims that a device resembling an earthquake detector existed in Ancient Egypt have no confirmation in reliable historical sources. How the central column inside the vessel opened only one dragon's mouth is not known.
A seismoscope is an instrument that shows that the ground has shaken, without the continuous record that a seismometer keeps.

Part of the star catalogue can be traced to Hipparchus rather than Ptolemy: about 18 to 20 errors are also found in Hipparchus's catalogue, and some attempts at dating the observations point to his time.
The Almagest is the astronomical treatise of Claudius Ptolemy, written in Greek in Alexandria around 150 CE.
An older view gave it an eastern origin, in Arab seafaring.
A lateen is a triangular sail set on a long yard mounted at an angle on the mast and running fore and aft; it originated in the Mediterranean as early as the 2nd century CE, in Roman times.

A possible earlier inscription, the Meldorf fibula, dates to around 50 CE, and Tacitus's Germania, from around 98 CE, may describe the use of rune-like inscriptions. Raetic, Venetic, Etruscan and Old Latin scripts have all been proposed as the immediate source.
Runes are the letters of a set of related alphabets, known as rune-rows or futharks, native to the Germanic peoples.
Its origin is disputed: Kuhn and Cheng argue for China, where dictionaries of the 2nd century CE mention it; others place it in India, or in the Middle East, where it was known by 1030.

The spinning wheel is a device in which a hand- or foot-turned wheel drives the spindle that spins fibres into thread or yarn; its origin is disputed, and some scholars hold that Chinese dictionaries of the 2nd century CE mention it.
Galen was a Greek physician of the second century CE whose writings dominated medicine for centuries.
These were prints on silk; the earliest prints on paper date from about 650–670, and the Diamond Sutra of 868 is the oldest dated printed book.
Woodblock printing is a technique of printing text or images by carving them in relief on a wooden block, inking it and pressing paper onto it.
The dating of its oldest witness, the Bakhshali manuscript, is disputed; the first dated, undisputed zero is the Gwalior inscription of 876.
The Hindu–Arabic numeral system is the decimal place-value system of writing numbers with ten digits, including zero, used throughout the world today.
Its date is much debated: its composition may have begun in the last centuries BCE, and proposals range from 2000 BCE to the 6th century CE.
The Sushruta Samhita is an ancient Sanskrit treatise on medicine and surgery attributed to Sushruta, one of the foundational texts of Ayurveda.
Toe loops were used in India by the 2nd century BCE, some credit the Sarmatians, and a single iron stirrup from Mongolia is dated 243–405 CE.
A stirrup is a light frame or ring hung by a strap from a saddle to hold a rider's foot, first known in China under the Jin dynasty in the early 4th century CE.
The earliest rowed true longship, the Nydam ship, dates to around 400 CE. Bronze Age rock carvings in Sweden show long animal-headed ships, which suggests a longer tradition of such vessels.

Longships were long, slender, clinker-built warships propelled by oars and later also by sail, used by the Norse and neighbouring Germanic peoples from at least the 4th century CE and throughout the Viking Age.
The first modern oil wells were drilled near Baku in 1846–1848.
An oil well is a hole bored into the Earth to bring petroleum to the surface; the earliest known were drilled in China in 347 CE.
Whether Ptolemy or earlier astronomers used it is debated, and its attribution to Hypatia rests on a misreading.

An astrolabe is an astronomical instrument that serves as a star chart and model of the visible sky, used to measure the altitude of stars and find latitude; it dates from classical antiquity, and Theon of Alexandria (c. 335–405) wrote a…

There is possible evidence of ondol at Unggi, North Korea, about 1000 BCE, and a Neolithic dwelling at Sonbong dated about 5000 BCE with a clear vestige of gudeul. It is also said that the oldest known ondol is of the 13th century CE, so the dating is inconsistent.
Ondol, or gudeul, is Korean traditional underfloor heating in which wood smoke from a firebox passes under a thick masonry floor and out through a freestanding chimney.
Sugarcane is a tall tropical grass whose stalks are crushed to produce sugar.

Four bronze horseshoes with what seem to be nail holes, found in an Etruscan tomb of around 400 BCE, may be older, and Catullus's 'mule shoes' may mean the Roman hipposandal rather than a nailed shoe; there is no hard evidence that the Druids invented it.
A horseshoe is a piece of equipment, usually nailed through the hoof wall, that protects a horse's hoof from wear.
The modern cotton gin is credited to Eli Whitney in 1793, though some credit Catharine Littlefield Greene with suggesting its brush.

The cotton gin is a machine that separates cotton fibres from their seeds; the earliest evidence of it is a single-roller gin depicted in 5th-century Buddhist paintings in the Ajanta Caves in western India.
Mesoamerica: south-central Mexico and Central America (earliest at Chiapa de Corzo, Chiapas)
Placeholder zeros are older, in Babylonian texts from about 700 BCE, and Ptolemy used a zero by 150 CE; Brahmagupta set out rules for calculating with zero in the 7th century.

Zero is the number for an empty quantity and the placeholder digit of positional notation, which in its modern use derives from India, where a Jain text internally dated to 458 CE uses a decimal place-value system including zero.
An earlier, doubtful depiction comes from a 3rd-century tomb in Sichuan, and some see a partial collar in ancient Rome.
A horse collar is a padded harness collar that spreads a load across a horse's shoulders and chest without pressing on its windpipe; it was invented in China by the early medieval period.
The kite has been claimed as the invention of the 5th-century BCE Chinese philosophers Mozi and Lu Ban, who are said to have flown wooden kites called muyuan.
A kite is a tethered craft heavier than air whose wing surfaces react against the wind to give lift.
A tide mill on the River Fleet in London may date to Roman times and is possibly the earliest in the Roman world.
A tide mill is a water mill driven by the rise and fall of the tide, which fills a mill pond through a one-way gate and releases the water to turn a wheel.
No record from the time of its building survives; the credit to Li Chun comes from later chronicles.

The Anji Bridge, or Zhaozhou Bridge, is a stone bridge over the Xiaohe River in Zhao County, Hebei, built in 595–605 under the Sui dynasty and credited to the craftsman Li Chun; it is the world's oldest open-spandrel segmental arch bridge…
Fire-carrying ships may predate Kallinikos’s arrival, and some think it was the work of the chemists of Constantinople rather than one man.
Greek fire was an incendiary weapon used by the Byzantine Empire, typically projected from siphons on warships, and able to burn on water.
Islamic glassmakers were inspired and active from the 8th century, and an Assyrian formula for coloured glass from Nineveh dates to the 7th century BCE; neither is dated as windows.
Stained glass is coloured glass, as a material or an art, made into windows from small pieces joined by lead strips called cames and held in a rigid frame.

Maya blue is a turquoise or azure blue pigment made by cultures of pre-Columbian Mesoamerica, such as the Maya and Aztecs, from about 800 CE; it combines indigo dye from the leaves of the anil plant with palygorskite, a natural clay.
A possible proto-quipu from Caral, of 3000–1800 BCE, has yet to be evaluated.

A quipu, or khipu, is a record-keeping device of knotted cords of cotton or camelid fibre, first undisputedly attested in the central Andes in the Middle Horizon, c. 600–1000 CE, when it was probably used by the Wari Empire.
Al-Walid I’s foundation at Damascus in 707 may have been a leprosarium rather than a hospital, and Harun al-Rashid’s traditional hospital of 787 is questioned.

A bimaristan is a hospital of the medieval Islamic world; the first true one was probably founded in Baghdad under the Abbasid caliph Harun al-Rashid, and the first documented general hospital arose there in 805.
Gunpowder is an explosive mixture of saltpetre, charcoal and sulphur, first developed in China.
Whether earlier work, from the Rhind papyrus to Diophantus and Brahmagupta, counts as algebra is debated.
Algebra is the branch of mathematics that deals with symbols and the rules for manipulating them to solve equations.
The modern industry began with lamp oil from coal: Abraham Gesner claimed priority from 1846 and James Young patented his process in 1850.

Kerosene, also called paraffin, is a combustible hydrocarbon liquid distilled from petroleum and used as a fuel for lamps, stoves and jet engines; the distilling of crude oil into kerosene was first written about in the 9th century by the…
Whether the vertical windmill of 12th-century Europe owed anything to the Persian one is unclear.
A windmill is a machine driven by wind acting on vanes or sails to grind grain or pump water, first known in Persia, where windmills were working in Khorasan in the 9th century.
Cyril and Methodius created the Glagolitic script but not Cyrillic itself; its name denotes homage rather than authorship, and Paul Cubberley places its development by their students in the 890s.

The Cyrillic script is a writing system developed during the 9th century at the Preslav Literary School in the First Bulgarian Empire, during the reign of Tsar Simeon I the Great, probably by disciples of the Byzantine brothers Cyril and…
The fire lance was an early gunpowder weapon: a tube of gunpowder, usually bamboo, strapped to a spear or other polearm, with the earliest evidence from China in 950.
Diodorus Siculus credits engineers of Ptolemy II with a lock in Egypt about 274 BCE, but not a pound lock.
A pound lock is a chamber with gates at both ends in which the water level is raised or lowered to move boats between levels of a waterway, first built in Song dynasty China by Qiao Weiyue in 984.
The Book of Optics is a seven-volume treatise on optics written between 1011 and 1021 by the medieval Arab scholar Ibn al-Haytham, known in the West as Alhazen (965–c. 1040).
Merchants in Sichuan issued the first notes, the jiaozi; the government took over their production in 1023.
Paper money is currency printed on paper rather than minted in metal.
The Canon of Medicine is an encyclopedia of medicine in five books compiled by Ibn Sina (Avicenna), begun in Gorganj and completed in Hamadan in 1025.
Whether Asian movable type influenced Gutenberg is debated.
Movable type is a printing system using individual, reusable characters that can be arranged to form texts.

Rudimentary incendiary grenades, jars of Greek fire, appeared in the Byzantine Empire not long after the reign of Leo III (717–741). The Wujing Zongyao's gunpowder shells are named only as a prototype, in Needham's view.
A grenade is a small explosive projectile thrown by hand or launched from a rifle attachment or launcher.
A lodestone “south-pointing spoon” for divination is attributed to the Han in the 2nd century BCE, but none has been found.
The magnetic compass is a navigational instrument that uses a magnetised needle to indicate direction.

Al-Razi may have made it without knowing in a recipe of his Book of Secrets. An Arabic treatise with a recipe for it, falsely attributed to Ja'far al-Sadiq, is dated to the thirteenth century by Julius Ruska but earlier by al-Hassan.
Sulfuric acid, called oil of vitriol by medieval alchemists, is a strong acid first made by distilling vitriols, the hydrated sulfates of metals.

The Garrett works at Leiston (1853) is called the first flow assembly line and the Portsmouth Block Mills (1801 to 1803) probably the earliest linear continuous assembly process of the industrial age; production line methods did not become common after the Arsenal. Credit for the modern line is divided among Ransom Olds (1901) and Ford's team (1913).
An assembly line is a manufacturing process in which the unfinished product moves in a direct line from workstation to workstation, with parts added in sequence until it is complete.

During the Han dynasty (202 BCE to 220 CE) people threw bamboo stems into a fire to produce a loud explosion, and later gunpowder in small containers imitated the sound, but these were firecrackers rather than fireworks of the Song kind.
Fireworks are low explosive pyrotechnic devices used for entertainment, most often in displays at celebrations.

A pottery model of a ship with a stern-mounted rudder from before the 1st century CE is already called a junk; the battened junk sail was probably Southeast Asian in origin, first shown at the Bayon temple at Angkor Thom.
A junk is a Chinese sailing ship with a central rudder, an overhanging flat transom, watertight bulkheads and a flat bottom, built with iron nails and clamps.
Culhuacan may have built the first chinampas about 1100; the Aztecs did not invent them but farmed them on a far larger scale.
A chinampa is an artificial agricultural plot built up from mud and vegetation in shallow lake beds, separated by canals.
The flying buttress was first developed in late antiquity: early, undated examples stand on the Basilica of San Vitale in Ravenna and the Rotunda of Galerius in Thessaloniki.
A flying buttress is a ramping arch that carries the outward thrust of a stone vault or roof from the upper part of a wall across open space to a massive pier standing away from it.
Where it was first built is not agreed: al-Tarsusi’s description of 1187 implies it was not new, and earlier cases have been argued from sieges between 1090 and 1165.
A counterweight trebuchet is a siege engine that uses a heavy falling weight to swing a throwing arm, capable of hurling large stones over long distances.

The 1211 ledger may imply the system began to evolve in the 12th century. Some sources suggest Giovanni di Bicci de' Medici introduced it for the Medici bank in the 14th century, though evidence for this is lacking.
Double-entry bookkeeping records every financial transaction with equal and opposite entries, debits and credits, so that the books balance.

A rocket is an elongated flying vehicle driven by a rocket engine, carrying all its propellant and so needing no surrounding air; gunpowder rockets evolved in China under the Song dynasty by the 13th century.
The name covered different hulls over the centuries; the ocean-going caravel of the voyages of exploration was developed in 15th-century Portugal.
A caravel was a small, highly manoeuvrable sailing ship, often with lateen sails that allowed it to sail close to the wind.
Estimates for the first true cannon run from about 1200 to 1280; the Xanadu Gun of 1298 is the oldest with a date inscribed.
A cannon is a large-calibre gun, a type of artillery firing a projectile with an explosive propellant, first securely attested in China in the 13th century.
A 17th-century claim that Salvino degli Armati of Florence invented them is false, and the suggested Chinese and Indian origins rest on later evidence.
Eyeglasses, or spectacles, are lenses held in a frame in front of the eyes; the first are estimated to have been made in central Italy, most likely in Pisa or Florence, by about 1290.
Derek de Solla Price held that the water-driven escapements of Tang China, built in 723–725, were the source of the Western escapement.
A mechanical clock is a timekeeping device driven by a mechanism such as falling weights or water and an escapement.
The invention is attributed to China, but only the 14th-century treatise and 16th-century records, with the first Western plan in 1574.
A naval mine, or sea mine, is a self-contained explosive weapon placed in water to damage or destroy ships or submarines, left to wait until triggered by the approach of or contact with a vessel.
Isolating the sick is far older, from the book of Leviticus to Ibn Sina’s Canon of Medicine; Ragusa held back newcomers who might carry plague.

Quarantine is a restriction on the movement of people, animals and goods to prevent the spread of disease or pests; a 30-day isolation of newcomers, the trentino, was first imposed by the Republic of Ragusa (modern Dubrovnik, Croatia) in…

The hwacha was a Korean weapons platform, a wooden cart carrying a launch pad, first built in 1409 under the Joseon dynasty; it could fire up to 200 rocket-powered arrows, or volleys of arrows and bolts from gun barrels.
The matchlock arquebus appeared shortly before 1475 in Europe, or by 1465 in the Ottoman Empire; its origin is disputed.
The arquebus was an early form of matchlock firearm used from the fifteenth to the seventeenth century.
Admiral Yi Sun-sin used an improved design against the Japanese invasions of 1592–1598; whether it was armoured with iron plates is disputed.
The turtle ship (geobukseon) was a Korean warship named after its covering, said to resemble a turtle's shell, and first recorded in 1413 in the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty.
It was built to the plans of the earlier Maragheh observatory.
The Ulugh Beg Observatory was an astronomical observatory built in Samarkand in the 1420s by the Timurid ruler Ulugh Beg.

Part of the network was built by earlier cultures, notably the Wari in northern central Peru and the Tiwanaku in Bolivia (the Tiwanaku civilisation lasted between the 6th and 12th centuries CE); no date is given for those roads.
The Qhapaq Ñan was the road network of the Inca Empire, some 40,000 kilometres long, running along the Andes and the Pacific coast from present-day Colombia to Chile and Argentina.
Printing is the mechanical reproduction of text and images.
When work on it began is unknown, and whether scripts such as ʼPhags-pa influenced its letters is debated.
Hangul is the Korean alphabet, created in 1443 under King Sejong of Joseon and promulgated in 1446 as the Hunminjeongeum, "the proper sounds for instructing the people".

The 10th-century physician al-Razi wrote of bunchum, which later accounts say was made from a root. Legends credit the discovery to Kaldi, a 9th-century goatherd, or to the 13th-century Sufi al-Shadhili.
Coffee is a drink brewed from the roasted seeds of the coffee plant, which grows wild in Ethiopia.
No date for the first bridges is known; they were part of the road system of the Inca Empire (1438–1533).
Inca rope bridges are simple suspension bridges of woven grass that the Inca Empire built over canyons, gorges and rivers as part of its road system.

In 852 Armen Firman jumped from a tower in Córdoba wearing a large cloak; Faust Vrančić's jump of 1617 from St Mark's Campanile in Venice probably never took place. The first recorded jump with a parachute was Lenormand's in 1783.
A parachute is a device that slows an object's descent through an atmosphere by creating drag.
The Norfolk four-course system is a method of crop rotation in which four crops follow one another over a four-year cycle: wheat, turnips, barley, and clover or ryegrass.
Gaspard Kollner of Vienna made spiral-grooved barrels as early as 1498 by some accounts, but some scholars hold that his grooves were straight until Kotter helped him.
Rifling is the helical grooving cut inside a gun barrel to spin the projectile, steadying its flight and making it more accurate.
It may have been little more than a new name for a heavy arquebus; the word is recorded from 1499.
The musket is a muzzle-loading, smoothbore firearm that became the standard infantry weapon in many armies from the sixteenth to the nineteenth century.
The more than 250 illustrations are generally attributed by modern scholars to the 'studio of Titian' rather than to Johannes Stephanus of Calcar, who drew for Vesalius's earlier tracts.
De humani corporis fabrica is a set of seven books on human anatomy by Andreas Vesalius, based on his lectures at Padua and printed by Johannes Oporinus in Basel in 1543.
De Humani Corporis Fabrica Libri Septem
Some sources date it to the 11th century in China, and claims of an ancient Indian origin are disputed.

Variolation was the deliberate infection of a person with material from a smallpox patient, usually rubbed into scratches in the skin or, in China, blown up the nose as powdered scabs, to cause a mild illness that gave immunity; its…
Taqi al-Din’s turbine turned a roasting spit; the modern steam turbine was invented by Charles Parsons in 1884.

A steam turbine is a heat engine that extracts energy from pressurised steam to turn a rotating shaft; Taqi al-Din described one that turned a spit in Ottoman Egypt in 1551, after the aeolipile of Hero of Alexandria.
Some sources date the discovery of the Borrowdale graphite as early as 1500.
A pencil is a writing or drawing implement with a solid core of pigment, usually graphite, in a protective casing.
The Mercator projection is a way of drawing the globe on a flat map in which courses of constant compass bearing, rhumb lines, appear as straight lines, so that a chart serves sailors directly.
The Gregorian leap-year rule of 97 leap years in 400 years was put forward by Petrus Pitatus of Verona in 1560.
The Gregorian calendar went into effect in October 1582 under the papal bull Inter gravissimas, issued on 24 February 1582 by Pope Gregory XIII, as a reform of the Julian calendar.

A revolving three-barrelled matchlock pistol in Venice dates from at least 1548, and a Tower of London matchlock revolver once believed to be 15th century is an Indian matchlock of the 1800s. Samuel Colt's 1836 patent is credited with the first modern practical revolver, though earlier similar examples existed.
A revolver is a repeating handgun with a revolving cylinder holding several chambers, each aligned in turn with the barrel.
A hearing aid is a device that improves hearing by making sound audible to a person with hearing loss.
Court gazettes circulated earlier in Tang China, and a printed daily, the Jobo, appeared in Joseon Korea in 1577.

A newspaper is a periodical publication of written news about current events; the German-language Relation, printed from 1605 by Johann Carolus in Strasbourg, in the Holy Roman Empire, is often recognised as the first.
The word bayonette is older, from the 16th century, but it is unclear whether it then named a knife fitted to a gun; its supposed origin in the town of Bayonne has no basis in fact.
A bayonet is a knife, dagger, sword or spike mounted on the barrel of a musket or rifle, so that the gun can be used as a spear in close combat.
Ayanz patented a steam-powered pump in 1606; Thomas Savery’s pump of 1698 was the first commercial steam device, and Thomas Newcomen’s engine of about 1712 the first to drive machinery.

A steam engine is a heat engine that does mechanical work with steam, usually by pushing a piston in a cylinder; the Spanish inventor Jerónimo de Ayanz patented the first steam-powered water pump, for draining mines, in 1606.
The actual inventor is unknown; Lipperhey’s patent application of 1608 is the earliest record of a telescope.

A telescope is an instrument for observing distant objects by the radiation they emit, absorb or reflect; the first known practical telescopes, refractors with glass lenses, were invented in the Netherlands at the beginning of the 17th…
Kepler's laws of planetary motion give good approximations for the orbits of planets around the Sun.
Firearms with some form of flint ignition were in use for over half a century before: the snaplock was probably invented shortly before 1517 and was certainly in use by 1547.
A flintlock is a firearm that fires by striking a flint to make a spark, and the name also covers the mechanism itself.

A logarithm is the exponent to which a fixed number, the base, must be raised to produce a given number; logarithms were introduced by John Napier in 1614, in his book Mirifici Logarithmorum Canonis Descriptio, as a means of simplifying…
The inventor is unknown; claims have been made for Zacharias Janssen in the Netherlands, for Cornelis Drebbel and for Galileo.

A microscope is an instrument for examining objects too small to be seen by the naked eye; the earliest known compound microscopes, which combine an objective lens near the specimen with an eyepiece, appeared in Europe around 1620.
Drebbel’s oar-driven boat was a submersible; David Bushnell’s Turtle of 1775 was the first verified submarine able to move underwater on its own.

A submarine is a watercraft capable of independent operation underwater; the first submersible of which reliable information exists, propelled by oars, was built in 1620 by Cornelis Drebbel, a Dutchman in the service of James I of England.

Oughtred became involved in a vitriolic controversy over priority with his one-time student Richard Delamain; his own ideas were made public only in publications of his student William Forster in 1632 and 1653.
A slide rule is a hand-operated mechanical calculator of slidable rulers, used for multiplication, division, roots, logarithms and trigonometry.
Galileo is often said to be the inventor, but no surviving document shows that he made such an instrument. Jean Leurechon described one with a scale of 8 degrees in 1624.
A thermometer measures temperature through a change in a sensor that is read against a scale.
Ibn al-Nafis had described the pulmonary circulation in the 13th century and Michael Servetus in 1553; the complete circulation is Harvey’s.
De Motu Cordis is William Harvey's treatise on the motion of the heart and blood, first published in 1628, which established that the blood circulates through the body.
Exercitatio Anatomica de Motu Cordis et Sanguinis in Animalibus
The alkaloid itself was isolated in 1820 by Pierre Joseph Pelletier and Joseph Bienaimé Caventou; the story that the Countess of Chinchón brought the bark to Europe is a myth.

Quinine is an alkaloid from the bark of the cinchona tree, native to Peru, used to treat malaria; extracts of the bark were used against malaria from at least 1632, and the substance itself was first isolated in 1820 by the French…
The Pascaline, or Pascal's calculator, is a mechanical calculator invented by Blaise Pascal in 1642, the first operational mechanical calculator with better tens-carry.

The 1643 date was suggested only after Torricelli's death. Gasparo Berti built a rudimentary water barometer between 1640 and 1644, and René Descartes described an experiment to measure atmospheric pressure as early as 1631, with no evidence that he built one.
A barometer is an instrument that measures air pressure, from which changes in the weather can be forecast.

The suction pump that preceded it dates to antiquity: dual-action suction pumps were found at Pompeii, and al-Jazari described them in the 13th century. These did not produce a measurable vacuum, which was first understood in the 17th century.
A vacuum pump draws gas particles from a sealed volume to leave a partial vacuum.

A pendulum clock is a clock that uses a swinging weight, the pendulum, as its timekeeping element; it was invented on 25 December 1656 by the Dutch scientist Christiaan Huygens, inspired by Galileo Galilei's investigations of pendulums…

Cardano's analysis of games of chance in the sixteenth century and the work of Fermat and Pascal on the problem of points in the seventeenth century came before Huygens's book; no year is given for them, so the first firm date is the book's.
Probability theory, or probability calculus, is the branch of mathematics concerned with probability, treated rigorously through a set of axioms.
Girolamo Fracastoro proposed a basic form in 1546; the theory prevailed only after the work of Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch in the late 19th century.

The germ theory of disease is the scientific theory that microorganisms, known as pathogens or germs, can cause disease; Athanasius Kircher was the first to attribute infectious disease to a microscopic pathogen, in his Scrutinium…

Lower's transfusion was between two dogs; the first from an animal to a human was Jean-Baptiste Denys's in France in 1667, and the first successful one of human blood James Blundell's in London in 1818.
Blood transfusion is the transfer of blood or its components into the veins of a human or other animal.
Newton derived his results in 1665–1666 but Leibniz published first, in 1684; they reached them independently, though the credit was bitterly disputed.
Calculus is the branch of mathematics that studies continuous change, formulated independently by Isaac Newton and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz in 17th-century Europe.
A medical or clinical thermometer measures the body temperature of a human or other animal.
Spectroscopy is the field of study that measures and interprets electromagnetic spectra as they interact with matter.

Binary-like systems appear in ancient Egypt (Horus-Eye fractions, early forms c. 2400 BCE), in the Chinese I Ching, in Pingala's description of metres in India (c. 2nd century BCE) and in Ifá divination. Thomas Harriot investigated binary before Leibniz but did not publish.
