A binary number is a number expressed in the base-2 numeral system, which uses only the symbols 0 and 1 and is a positional notation with a radix of 2.
Galvanic paint, a precursor to hot-dip galvanising, was patented by Stanislas Sorel of Paris on 10 June 1837, the date most often associated with the process.
Galvanisation is the process of applying a protective zinc coating to steel or iron to prevent rusting, most often by dipping parts in a bath of molten zinc.
Robert Hooke claimed priority for the inverse-square law of gravity, which Newton denied.

Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica, usually called the Principia, is Isaac Newton's treatise on mechanics, published in Latin in London in 1687 with the support of Edmond Halley and the Royal Society.

Bouchon's 1725 control used punched paper tape, not cards; chained cards date from Jacquard in 1804. Punched holes for control and storage were devised independently several times, among them Semyon Korsakov, who announced punched cards for storing and searching information in September 1832.
A punched card is a stiff paper medium that stores information by the presence or absence of holes in fixed positions.
Ranked classification goes back to Plato and Aristotle, and Linnaeus neither invented the concept nor gave it its present form; 'Linnaean taxonomy' does not exist as a single defined system.

Linnaean taxonomy is the form of biological classification set out by Carl Linnaeus in his Systema Naturae (1735) and later works, in which he described three kingdoms, animal, vegetable and mineral, each divided into classes, orders…
Long credited to Musschenbroek, it was first made by von Kleist; Cunaeus first discovered why the jar had to be held in the hand.
The Leyden jar is an electrical component that stores a high-voltage charge between conductors on the inside and outside of a glass jar, and was the original form of the capacitor.

Hourglass-shaped talking drums are said to be among the oldest instruments of West African griots and are traced back to the Bono, Yoruba, Hausa and the Ghana Empire, but no date is given for that earlier history; the earliest dated evidence is the notice taken by Europeans in the first half of the 18th century.
The talking drum is an hourglass-shaped drum from West Africa with two drumheads joined by leather tension cords.

Franklin conceived the rod in 1749 and was credited with the invention; whether Diviš's 1754 machine, meant to prevent thunderstorms, counts as an independent invention is debated. The Nevyansk Tower (1721–1745) has a grounded metal rod, but its intent is unknown.
A lightning rod is a metal rod mounted on a structure to protect it from a lightning strike by conducting the current to ground.
Jacob Perkins built the first working vapour-compression system in 1834, and James Harrison the first practical one in 1851.

Refrigeration is the artificial cooling of a space, substance or system below the surrounding temperature; the harvesting of snow and ice is estimated to have begun before 1000 BCE, and artificial refrigeration began with a small machine…
Christiaan Huygens built a balance-spring chronometer in 1675 that kept poor time at sea, and some see Pierre Le Roy’s of 1766 as the basis of the modern chronometer.

A marine chronometer is a precision timepiece carried on a ship to find its longitude by comparing Greenwich Mean Time with local time, first developed in the 18th century: the Yorkshire carpenter John Harrison's H4 of 1761 solved the…
Thomas Highs of Leigh has claimed to be the inventor, and a myth credits Thomas Earnshaw with a similar device that he destroyed.
The spinning jenny is a multi-spindle spinning frame invented in 1764–1765 by James Hargreaves at Stanhill, Oswaldtwistle, in Lancashire, England.
The modern intermodal container dates from 1955 to 1956. The first container ship, the Autocarrier, was launched in February 1931, and 'loose boxes' for coal from the late 1780s.
Containerisation is a system of freight transport using standardised containers that can be moved between ships, trains and trucks without being opened.

Michael Sendivogius is said to have isolated the gas before 1604 and recognised it as a substance in air, but contemporaries did not understand his work. Priestley's work is often given priority because it was published first.
Oxygen is a chemical element with the symbol O and atomic number 8, a reactive nonmetal that makes up almost half of the Earth's crust in compounds.
Jan van Helmont's mid-17th-century weighing of soil and a growing plant led him to hypothesise that the plant's mass came from water; this is called partially accurate.
Photosynthesis is a system of biological processes by which autotrophic organisms such as most plants, algae and cyanobacteria convert light energy, typically from sunlight, into chemical energy.

Sky lanterns, used for military signals by Zhuge Liang in the Three Kingdoms era, were a precursor; in 1709 Bartolomeu de Gusmão showed an unmanned demonstration of his Passarola to John V of Portugal at the Casa da Índia.
A hot air balloon is a lighter-than-air aircraft whose envelope holds heated air, with a basket or gondola for passengers and a source of heat hung beneath it.
This was the Pyroscaphe, the first working steamboat; the first sea-going steamship, Richard Wright’s Experiment, sailed in 1813.
A steamship is a ship powered by a steam engine.
Bleaching in bleachfields by sun and water is the earliest form, but no date is given for it; a large cloth bleaching industry existed in western Europe in the 17th century.
Bleach is any chemical product used to remove colour from fabric, fibre or food, or to disinfect.
Ideas for an automatic loom were developed in 1684 by M. de Gennes in Paris and by Vaucanson in 1745, but were forgotten; Cartwright's loom was not a commercial success.
A power loom is a mechanised loom that automates weaving by mechanical power, interlacing warp and weft threads through cams, gears, levers and pulleys.
Recent work sees a gradual change over two centuries, with Robert Boyle laying its foundations.

The chemical revolution was the reformulation of chemistry during the 17th and 18th centuries that culminated in the law of conservation of mass and the oxygen theory of combustion, long credited to the French chemist Antoine Lavoisier.
Chinese records dating back 1,700 years indicate natural gas carried by bamboo pipes for lighting and heating in homes.
Gas lighting is the production of artificial light by burning a fuel gas, principally coal gas in the period when it was widespread.
Robert Hooke outlined a visual telegraph in 1684, and the Chappe brothers first demonstrated theirs in 1791.

An optical telegraph is a line of stations, typically towers, that pass text along by visual signals; credit for the first successful one goes to the French engineer Claude Chappe and his brothers in 1792, and Chappe's word télégraphe…
John Barber’s gas turbine of 1791 came earlier; Nicolaus Otto’s four-stroke engine of 1876 was the first modern one.

An internal combustion engine is a heat engine in which fuel burns with air or another oxidiser inside the engine, and the expanding gases push directly on pistons, turbine blades, a rotor or a nozzle; Robert Street patented one in 1794.

Lithography is a planographic method of printing based on the immiscibility of oil and water: an image drawn with a greasy substance on smooth limestone or a metal plate takes the oily ink, while the wetted, etched surface around it…
Benjamin Jesty and others had tried cowpox inoculation from 1774; Jenner was the first to publish the evidence.

The smallpox vaccine is the first vaccine developed against a contagious disease: in 1796 the British physician Edward Jenner showed that infection with the mild cowpox virus gave immunity to smallpox; his Inquiry of 1798 presented cowpox…

Around 1665–1670 Gabriel Mouton suggested replacing France's many units with a single decimal system based on a minute of arc of the Earth; his ideas were clearly the basis of the 1790s system, though his contribution is sometimes overlooked.
The metric system standardises base units and names large and small quantities with decimal prefixes such as kilo and milli.

The voltaic pile is a stack of paired metal discs separated by brine-soaked cloth or cardboard, the first electrical battery that could continuously provide an electric current; it was invented by the Italian chemist Alessandro Volta, who…

In 1785 Martinus van Marum reduced tin, zinc and antimony from their salts with an electrostatic generator without knowing the process, and in 1789 Adriaan Paets van Troostwijk and Jan Rudolph Deiman split small amounts of water; Johann Ritter also demonstrated it in 1800.
Electrolysis is the use of a direct electric current to drive a chemical reaction that would not otherwise occur, as in separating elements from ores and compounds.
Credit for the first practical bulb is disputed between Thomas Edison, whose first successful test was in 1879, and Joseph Swan, whose bulbs were in use in London by 1881.

An incandescent light bulb is an electric light in which current heats a filament until it glows inside an evacuated or gas-filled glass bulb; Humphry Davy made an electric incandescent light in 1802 at the Royal Institution of Great…
Who deserves the most credit for general anaesthesia is debated.

General anaesthesia is a drug-induced loss of consciousness from which a patient cannot be roused even by pain; the first successful surgery on record under it was performed by the Japanese surgeon Hanaoka Seishū on 14 November 1804.
The idea of indivisible particles is ancient, but as philosophy rather than science.

Atomic theory is the scientific theory that matter is composed of particles called atoms, set out in its modern form by John Dalton, who explained it to Thomas Thomson in 1804 and published his own version in 1808.

The article says the machine was based on earlier inventions by Basile Bouchon (1725), Jean Baptiste Falcon (1728) and Jacques Vaucanson (1740), that Jacquard 'possibly combined mechanical elements of other inventors, but certainly innovated', and that a first prototype of a Jacquard-type loom was made in the second half of the 15th century by an Italian weaver known as Jean le Calabrais.

The Jacquard machine is a device fitted to a loom that automates the weaving of complex patterns such as brocade and damask, controlled by a chain of punched cards; it was patented by Joseph Marie Jacquard in 1804.
United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

Thomas Saint's design of 1790, generally considered the first sewing machine, was never constructed; Josef Madersperger began work in 1807 and showed a machine in 1814; Thimonnier's of 1829 was the first practical one.
A sewing machine sews fabric and other materials together with thread.
Trevithick’s Coalbrookdale locomotive of 1802 may have run earlier, but no record of it working survives.

A steam locomotive is a self-propelled steam engine on wheels that moves itself and other vehicles by expanding steam; it was first developed in the United Kingdom, where on 21 February 1804 one of Richard Trevithick's locomotives made…

Research from the 1930s theorised that electroplating had been performed in the Parthian Empire with a device like the Baghdad Battery, but this has since been refuted: the items were fire-gilded using mercury.

Electroplating is a process that coats an object with metal by passing a direct electric current through a solution of a salt of that metal, so that the metal's cations are reduced onto the object, which serves as the cathode.
United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland
The Mumbles line was a one-off, and no street tramway appeared in Britain until 1860, when George Francis Train built one in Birkenhead. Records of a Baltimore street railway date from 1828.
A tram is an urban rail transit vehicle that runs on tracks on or beside public streets.
The Dutch navy was reported to carry salmon in tin-plated iron boxes as early as 1772; the tin can patented by Durand in 1810 was allegedly the idea of the Frenchman Philippe de Girard.
Canning is a method of preserving food by processing it and sealing it in an airtight container, a glass jar or a steel or tin can.
United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland
Georges-Louis Le Sage had an electric telegraph working between two rooms in 1774; the first commercial system, Cooke and Wheatstone’s, dates from 1837.
The telegraph was a system for transmitting messages over long distances by electrical signals along wires, developed in the nineteenth century.
The stethoscope is a medical device for listening to the sounds of the heart, lungs and intestines and to blood flow, a practice called auscultation.
Drais’s running machine had no pedals; they were added in France in the early 1860s.
A bicycle is a pedal-driven, single-track vehicle with two wheels attached to a frame, one behind the other.

Brunel is said to have been inspired by the shell of the shipworm. Alfred Ely Beach had suggested a circular design in 1840 and built one in 1869, but Greathead is credited with the first cylindrical shield in use.
A tunnelling shield is a protective structure used while excavating tunnels through soft, liquid or otherwise unstable ground, supporting the face until a permanent lining can be built.
The Cherokee syllabary is a writing system invented by Sequoyah in the late 1810s and early 1820s to write the Cherokee language.
Andrew Gordon and Benjamin Franklin described electrostatic motors in the 1740s and 1750s, but these were never put to practical use; Faraday's device of 1821 was the first electromagnetic one.
An electric motor is a machine that converts electrical energy into mechanical energy, usually through the interaction of a magnetic field and the current in a wire winding.
Braille is a tactile writing system used by blind and visually impaired people, in which characters are formed by six raised dots arranged in two columns of three, the braille cell.

The name Portland cement was recorded in a directory of 1823 with a William Lockwood. Aspdin’s cement has been called a proto-Portland cement: his son William is regarded as the inventor of the modern form, and Isaac Charles Johnson claimed to be its real father.

Portland cement is a hydraulic cement made by heating limestone and clay minerals in a kiln to form clinker, then grinding it with a little gypsum; it is the most common cement and the basic ingredient of concrete and mortar.
Its history as a discipline is said to begin with Otto von Guericke's vacuum pump of 1650; the first and second laws emerged together in the 1850s from the work of Rankine, Clausius and Thomson.
Thermodynamics is the branch of physics dealing with heat, work and temperature and their relation to energy, entropy and the properties of matter.

The article notes that Johann Heinrich Schulze's fleeting images of stencilled letters, about 1717, are 'sometimes regarded as the very first form of photography', that Thomas Wedgwood made the first reliably documented attempt to capture camera images around 1800 but could not fix them, and that Hippolyte Bayard developed a method of his own but was not recognised as its inventor because he delayed announcing it.

Photography, whose name means 'drawing of light', is the capture of camera images on light-sensitive materials; the first such image to be fixed was made by the French scientist Nicéphore Niépce in 1826 or 1827, after an exposure of hours…

Walker may have made his first friction matches during experiments in 1826. Earlier French friction lighters, Cagniard de la Tour’s phosphorus bottle of 1810 and François Derosne’s briquet phosphorique of 1816, proved inconvenient and unsafe.
A friction match is a small stick tipped with a mixture that ignites when struck against a rough surface.

Gallic reapers, which combed off the heads of grain, were used in Roman times in what is now France. Cyrus McCormick claimed to have invented his reaper in 1831, and an 1861 ruling of the United States Patent and Trademark Office gave much of the credit to Obed Hussey.
A mechanical reaper is a machine that cuts, and often gathers, grain crops at harvest.
Whether it overthrew vitalism, the source of its fame, is disputed.
The Wöhler synthesis is the conversion of ammonium cyanate into urea, described by Friedrich Wöhler in 1828 and often cited as the starting point of modern organic chemistry.
The self-excited dynamo was invented independently by Wheatstone, Siemens and Varley in 1866–1867.

An electric generator is a machine that converts mechanical energy into electrical energy; the first electromagnetic generator, the Faraday disk, was built by the British scientist Michael Faraday in 1831, a copper disc turning between…

Electromagnetic induction is the production of an electromotive force across an electrical conductor in a changing magnetic field; Michael Faraday is generally credited with its discovery, first demonstrated on 29 August 1831 with two…

Pixii's alternator came first, but alternating current became practical for power only with the transformers of the 1880s; from late 1887 Thomas Edison campaigned against it as too dangerous in the war of the currents.
Alternating current is an electric current that periodically reverses direction, the form in which electric power is delivered to homes and businesses.
The combine harvester is a machine that joins reaping, threshing or winnowing and gathering in a single process.
Efficient, practical transformer designs did not appear until the 1880s: the closed-core design of Zipernowsky, Bláthy and Déri dates from 1884–1885.
A transformer transfers electrical energy between circuits through a varying magnetic flux in a shared core.
The Analytical Engine is a design for a mechanical general-purpose computer by the English mathematician Charles Babbage, first described in 1837 as the successor to his difference engine.
The alphabet that carries Morse's name was Alfred Vail's, who extended Morse's numerals-only design in 1840, and most of the present international code comes from Friedrich Gerke's revision of 1848.
Morse code is a method of telecommunication that encodes letters, numerals and punctuation as standard sequences of two signal durations, dots and dashes.
Christian Friedrich Schönbein described a crude fuel cell of his own, in a letter of December 1838 published in June 1839.
A fuel cell is an electrochemical cell that converts the chemical energy of a fuel, often hydrogen, and an oxidising agent into electricity through a pair of redox reactions.
Schleiden claimed as his own an idea Barthélemy Dumortier had stated earlier, and Rudolf Virchow’s third tenet of 1855 had already been proposed by Robert Remak.

Cell theory is the scientific theory that living organisms are made up of cells, that the cell is their basic unit, and that all cells come from pre-existing cells; it was first formulated in 1839 by Matthias Jakob Schleiden for plants…
The first practical solar cell was demonstrated at Bell Laboratories in 1954.

A solar cell, or photovoltaic cell, is an electronic device that converts the energy of light directly into electricity through the photovoltaic effect; the French physicist Edmond Becquerel built the first in 1839.

Thomas Hancock took out a British patent for vulcanization with sulfur on 21 November 1843, eight weeks before Goodyear’s US patent of 30 January 1844; accounts differ on whether Hancock had studied samples of Goodyear’s rubber.
Vulcanization is the hardening of rubber, originally of natural rubber treated with sulfur and heat, which forms cross-links between its polymer chains and makes it firmer and more durable.
United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

In April 1680 William Dockwra established the London Penny Post, which used a hand stamp on the letter itself; many historians consider it the first postage stamp. In 1835 Lovrenc Košir of Ljubljana suggested pressed paper wafers as stamps, but the proposal was not adopted. Accounts vary as to who invented the adhesive stamp.
A postage stamp is a small piece of paper sold by a postal administration to show that postage has been paid.
United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland
Bain's patent is given as 1843 but his laboratory reproduction of graphic signs to 1846; the first commercial service, Caselli's, began in 1865.
Fax, short for facsimile, is the transmission of scanned printed text and images by telephone to a printer at the other end.
United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland
Dunlop's 1888 tyre is often given as the first, but in 1892 his patent was declared invalid because of Thomson's earlier patents (London 1845, France 1846, USA 1847).
A tyre is a ring-shaped component that surrounds a wheel's rim, carries the vehicle's load to the ground and provides traction.
In 1784 Jean-Pierre Blanchard fitted a hand-powered propeller to a balloon, the first recorded means of propulsion carried aloft, but not an engine-powered flight.
